source.title: On the Generalization of Models Trained with SGD: Information-Theoretic Bounds and Implications

record.file_problem: none; full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures gradient dispersion alongside training and test performance, and tests whether dynamic gradient clipping changes the gap. These are conceptual tests of generalization behavior, but the paper does not test the specific versions listed.
record.gate_note: The authors cite prior studies on memorization and regularization; cited results are not recorded. The Dropout and other regularizer comparisons in Table 1 and Table 2 are reported directly from Zheng et al. (2021), so they are not this study's results. Figure-only outcomes are not assigned precise values.
record.test_reason: The study reports generalization bounds, gradient-dispersion dynamics, and regularization experiments, but none directly tests V1–V8. Partial label corruption does not establish V1's random-label comparison; width sweeps report loss gaps without identifying interpolation or reporting classification test error; batch-size experiments measure bound terms rather than held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets. Dropout comparisons are borrowed results.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate but omits the main practical contribution: Gaussian model perturbation achieves competitive regularization performance. The bounds connect generalization to training trajectories and a flatness-related term; dispersion dynamics motivate clipping, which alleviates noisy-label overfitting without significant clean-data improvement. The appendix's statement that GMP is best on SVHN conflicts with Tables 1 and 2, where AMP scores higher.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops information-theoretic bounds for SGD, measures gradient dispersion, and evaluates dynamic gradient clipping and Gaussian model perturbation; it does not reproduce the listed original methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and label-noise level change the observed gradient-dispersion and accuracy dynamics. Learning rate and batch size change the trajectory and flatness terms in opposite directions; the authors describe the bound's relationship to those settings as complex.

fits_no_version.finding: Gradient dispersion exhibits epoch-wise phases associated with training/test accuracy divergence under partial label corruption. Clean CIFAR-10 test accuracy does not decline in the later phase.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient-dispersion dynamics can mark transitions between pattern learning and label memorization, depending on dataset and corruption.

fits_no_version.finding: Dynamic clipping slows memorization and reduces the accuracy gap under noisy labels; the authors report no significant improvement on clean datasets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dynamic gradient clipping can reduce noisy-label overfitting, with benefits dependent on label corruption.

fits_no_version.finding: The estimated information-theoretic bound decreases with model size and tracks the empirical loss-gap trend.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A trajectory-and-flatness bound can track loss-gap changes across network sizes.

fits_no_version.finding: GMP produces competitive classification accuracy using isotropic Gaussian parameter perturbations, with additional training cost.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Regularizing average loss under Gaussian parameter perturbations can improve image-classification performance.

record.problems: Several findings are presented only in figures without precise values in the text. Dynamic clipping is reported as not significantly improving generalization on clean datasets. The GMP comparisons for other methods are taken directly from Zheng et al. (2021), rather than run by this study.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: The paired natural-label and fully random-label experiment, including chance held-out accuracy with random labels; corruption here reaches only 60%.
Classification test-error trends beyond the width required for zero training error.
Matched convolutional versus fully connected comparisons and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer comparisons and tuning-dependent differences.
Held-out performance across batch sizes under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that recover performance.
Original dropout experiments; all reported dropout comparisons come from Zheng et al. (2021).
Magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance and its ranking of generalization gaps against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removal of highly memorized examples versus random removal followed by retraining.

record.verdict_notes: No claim-version verdicts are warranted. Figure-only presentation does not itself prevent qualitative assessment; the decisive issue is that these measures and comparisons do not establish the listed versions. The paper's epoch-wise double descent concerns gradient dispersion, rather than V2's width-dependent test error.

versions.untested_parts: The study varies the fraction of corrupted labels, but does not report the specified random-label held-out chance result alongside natural-label generalization for the same architectures and recipes.
Width is varied for the bound and empirical gap, but the study does not test widening past the width needed to fit labels while tracking test error.
The paper does not compare convolutional and fully connected networks on the same image task to test their generalization difference.
No adaptive optimizer comparison is reported.
Batch size is varied while plotting bound terms, but the paper does not report held-out performance comparisons under fixed epoch budgets.
Dropout results are cited from prior work, not produced by this study.
The paper studies gradient dispersion, not magnitude-aware sharpness or the ranking of generalization gaps against norm- and margin-based measures.
No training examples are removed or retrained on.

rows.measure: Gradient dispersion and training/testing accuracy over epochs; authors describe exponential decay of dispersion on the clean dataset and a small generalization gap in the initial training phase.
rows.note: The authors describe the clean-data dispersion as exponentially decaying; precise plotted values are not stated.
rows.check: Gradient dispersion and clean-label accuracy alone do not establish any listed version. Section E.1 specifies training to convergence without weight decay or batch normalization.

rows.operation_detail: Applied dynamic gradient clipping when the current gradient norm exceeded the norm from K steps earlier.
